searches.note: Twenty searches of a share of twenty eight, eight left for the run's shared allowance; one on Wittmann's cellar returned nothing on the house and is counted with it. Most were restricted to the VDP's own domain, a house's own domain or wein.plus and read as summaries. Writers' own sites that came up were read and never cited. No fetch tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites with their heights, aspects and soils, the making, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules.

The searches went first to the VDP's own site pages for every flagship vineyard and the sites named in others, then to the dates the stories turn on (1789, 1921, 2001 and 2000 for Keller; 1663, 1990 and 2004 for Wittmann; 1364, 1890 and 1925 for Gunderloch; 1934 and 1970 for Kühling-Gillot; 1991 and 2005 for Battenfeld-Spanier), then to the cellars.

Where the cellar rested on one trade account (a single Fuder for G-Max, cask sizes at Gunderloch, a parcel to a cask at Wittmann) it was replaced by the house's own words or cut back; where a site's place was wrong (the Zellerweg am Schwarzen Herrgott in Rheinhessen, not the Pfalz) it was corrected from the VDP.

tested: G-Max's name: the G for the present head's great grandfather Georg, who first bottled the family's Riesling in 1921, and Max for a son (elder or younger is disputed): Tastingbook and two trade accounts.
The first G-Max with the 2001 vintage: a wine wiki and a critic's vertical (writers' own sites, read, never cited), with Tastingbook's listing of a 2001.
1789 and the ancestor from Switzerland at the time of the Revolution, with property in the Hubacker: wein.plus and a trade directory.
VDP membership since 2000: the VDP's own estate pages, English and German. The takeover: 2000 vintage by German Wikipedia, 2001 by a trade profile.
The cellar: one wine wiki says wild yeast and an increasing turn to large old Fuder for the GGs; nothing read puts G-Max in one cask.
The Hubacker: the VDP's site page now names it Oberer Hubacker.

changed.why: One critic's report alone put G-Max in one cask; the wine wiki read speaks of the house's GGs in general.

changed.now: by most accounts on Wonnegau limestone (sites); parcels kept secret (table)
changed.why: The house names no parcel and one trade source places G-Max across the estate's sites.

changed.was: the 2001 vintage gave the first Grosses Gewächs and the first G-Max, made by the generation then taking over
changed.now: the first G-Max with 2001, a new generation taking the cellar around the turn of the century
changed.why: Only G-Max's first vintage is in two sources; the takeover is the 2000 vintage by German Wikipedia and 2001 by a trade profile.

changed.was: Dalsheimer Hubacker Riesling GG, a Grosses Gewächs since the 2001 vintage
changed.now: Dalsheim Hubacker Riesling GG, the Grosse Lage the VDP names the Oberer Hubacker

open: Whether Max is the elder or the younger son stays unsettled, so the record says only a son of the family named Max.
The theft from the Hubacker as the reason for the secret parcels rests on one account and stays hedged.
The comparison with Franz Keller of Baden was not searched; it is common knowledge of the trade.

tested: The Morstein on the VDP's pages: due south, 180 to 240 metres, 20 to 25 per cent, clay marl with limestone over limestone rock with an aquifer; first recorded as Marsten in 1282 in a gift to Otterberg. All in the record, confirmed.
1663, organic from 1990 and biodynamic from 2004: the house's page, Wikipedia and merchants; the VDP interview says the end of the 1980s for organic.
The cellar: the house's sheet says most wines ferment in traditional old oak; a German magazine notes wild fermentation and wood across the house. Parcel to a cask not found.
Aulerde and Brunnenhäuschen on the VDP's site pages.

changed.was: old oak in the vaulted cellar, each cask holding one parcel, on its lees
changed.now: the house's sheet: most wines in traditional old oak; by trade accounts wild yeast
changed.why: Parcel to a cask, the vaulted cellar and the lees were in nothing read.

open: Organic certification is 1990 on the house's page and several merchants, the end of the 1980s in the VDP's interview; the record follows 1990 as the house's account.

tested: The Rothenberg on the VDP's pages: the northernmost Roter Hang site, up to 75 per cent, coarse red clayey slate, little topsoil, bedrock near the surface, first recorded as in dem Rode in 1364.

1890, a banker of Mainz, the manor house; Zuckmayer's Der fröhliche Weinberg of 1925 with Jean Baptist Gunderloch, and the Jean Baptiste Kabinett: Wikipedia, wein.plus and a German blog's anniversary piece.
The cellar on the house's own page: long skin contact, slow natural fermentation in oak and stainless steel, long on the full lees, no additives; no cask sizes.
The Geisenheim Rothenberg exists as a separate VDP site.

changed.was: wild yeast in large old oak of 1,200 to 2,400 litres after slow pressing, no clarification
changed.now: long skin contact, slow natural fermentation in oak and stainless steel, long on full lees, no additives
changed.why: The house's own page says so; the cask sizes rested on trade accounts and a third account disagreed.

changed.was: Rheinhessen's one stretch of steep riverside rock
changed.now: a stretch of steep red rock above the river
changed.why: A claim of the only one, unsourced; Bingen's Scharlachberg is steep riverside rock too.

changed.was: given skin contact before fermenting in old oak
changed.now: red slate facing east to south east over the Rhine
changed.why: The cellar note was unsourced; the VDP's Pettenthal page gives slate and aspect.

open: The founder's dates (1846 to 1935) are in one source read, so he stays described, not named.

tested: The Pettenthal on the VDP's pages: east to south east, a small part due south, up to 70 per cent in its upper reaches, iron rich fine grained red clayey slate. Confirmed.
1970 for the Gillot marriage: a German listing; the early 1970s by a merchant; a blog dates it to the 1970 marriage of the parents of the present generation.

The 1934 ungrafted Rothenberg vines on the house's own pages: planted before the phylloxera protection laws, spared the land consolidation of the 1960s by their isolated position. The house does not say they escaped the louse.
Holdings in Pettenthal, Hipping, Ölberg and Rothenberg: wein.plus and the house.

changed.was: the 1934 vines escaped both phylloxera and the land consolidation of the 1960s
changed.now: by the house's account, its isolated position spared it the land consolidation of the 1960s
changed.why: The house says only that the vines were planted before the phylloxera protection laws.

changed.was: warmer and broader than the Pettenthal
changed.now: worked beside the Pettenthal and the Hipping

open: The double name's year is 1970 by wein.plus and a German listing, the early 1970s by a merchant; the question keys 1970 as the wine guide's account.
The marriage that joined the two estates' work is given as the 2000s; sources say 2005 and 2006.

tested: 1991 and organic from the start: the house's fact sheets of 2024 and 2025 and its thirtieth anniversary piece of 2021; one trade profile says 1998. Biodynamic from 2005: the house.

The Frauenberg on the VDP's page: south east, 190 to 270 metres, 10 to 40 per cent, shell limestone, limestone rock, loess, loam and marl; the house says south, 190 to 200 metres, limestone gravel over pure limestone.

The Zellerweg am Schwarzen Herrgott on the VDP's page: at Mölsheim in Rheinhessen near the Pfalz border, south south east, limestone; the Schwarzer Herrgott of the Zellertal is a separate Pfalz Grosse Lage. The record had it in the Pfalz: wrong.
The Kirchenstück at Hohen-Sülzen as a VDP Grosse Lage worked by the house: the VDP's listing.

changed.was: the Zellerweg am Schwarzen Herrgott across the border in the Zellertal of the Pfalz, a Pfalz wine
changed.now: at Mölsheim on the Rheinhessen side of the border; the trap now parts it from the Schwarzer Herrgott of the Zellertal, a separate Pfalz Grosse Lage
changed.why: The VDP's site pages place the Zellerweg at Mölsheim in Rheinhessen and list the Schwarzer Herrgott of the Zellertal separately in the Pfalz.

swaps.why: The house gives each of its Grosse Lagen its own page and nothing read sets the wurzelecht above the Pettenthal as its flagship; Gunderloch's record already teaches the Nackenheim Rothenberg, so a second Rothenberg would cost the group the Pettenthal, a third Roter Hang site; the wurzelecht keeps first place in others and a card.
